turn_text: Sure. Well, the House Democracy Partnership has somewhat different historical origins. It goes back to this kind of effort, member to member, staff to staff this kind of effort to focus as colleagues on parliamentary effectiveness and to work with the parliament's in emerging democracy situations to increase the effectiveness of their institutions. This dates back to Eastern and Central Europe in the early 90s when communism was falling and the Soviet Union was dissolving. All kinds of countries had to take showcase parliaments and actually make them work. And colleague of mine, Martin Frost of Texas had a great idea back then that we should reach out in quite direct ways. Member to member staff to staff to help bring these parliaments along. And the effort back then focused very heavily on research capacity, libraries, IT, But our staff went over for weeks at a time to work and getting those parliaments up and running. And we made a lot of visits ourselves. And I was a very junior member at that point. And that left a very lasting impression on me. New Gingrich let the whole thing expire when he came in in the mid-90s. So I tried for years to get this back up and running. And finally succeeded 15 years ago with the help of Republican Speaker Dennis Haster. And he appointed David Dreyer to chair the commission that I became chairman when Democrats took over in, you know, in 2007. And we've maintained a back part as an effort ever since. We still have a lot of focus on Eastern and Central Europe. We work, for example, in Macedonia, Kosovo, Georgia, Armenia, Ukraine. But we also have a worldwide focus with countries like Indonesia and Kenya and Peru, countries that are, yes, they're struggling, but they've also shown a real commitment and a real capacity to become functioning representative democracies. And we think that they and we have a mutual stake in making sure that that works. We have a mantra that Yes, democracy is about free and fair elections. But what happens between elections is really maybe what will matter in a lot of cases. And in that period between elections, that's when representative institutions either work or they don't. And the result of their efforts make a huge difference for whether democracy takes over.

And those discussions tend to focus on Newt Gingrich and the major changes that he undertook when he came in as a speaker after the 1994 wave election. And there's some truth at that. I mean, I was here a few years before that and I saw how much Republican politics shifted when when Gingrich first got into power when he displaced the rather amiable and moderate Bob Michael and became I think Republican whip was his first position but anyway it changed things once Gingrich came on the scene and certainly when he became speaker. However, I think A little broader view would suggest that this didn't happen in a vacuum. In fact, there had been some trends towards centralization in both parties for a number of years before that. On the Democratic side, there was what some political scientists call a responsible party impulse, which tried to reign in the Southern Conservative Committee chairs and subject the Democratic leadership of the House to more discipline and more of a policy focus. And honestly, a more progressive approach to national politics rooted in civil rights and other other issues. And so there was a centralization that sought to downplay some of these reactionary committee chairs at the fiefdoms that they held and to make the house more responsive to policy needs. And then along with that came more partisanship, more polarization, Both parties became more homogeneous internally, but further apart from each other. And so, and of course, Gingrich fomited that, but it wasn't just top down. It was also happening in the country and still happens in the country where the party bases are more divided than any of us can ever remember before. So just the basic fact is that a polarized institution and a more conflict-ridden institution requires more centralized leadership. So there's a reason that most members understand that this can't be the committee-centric, less partisan institution than it used to be if any of us wish it could be. And to your point, individual members often thrive in a less centralized institution where the committees really do most of the work and where people work across party lines. I started out here in the last stages of that kind of institution and I had some successes in a kind of a bill becomes a law fashion. I got some bills through on the basis that I'm describing, working through the committee process. But that has become more difficult. And so it's not just the leaders like Newt Gingrich or Nancy Pelosi or anybody else come in and want to be centralizing figures. To some extent, their institutional setting demands that of them. There's always an interaction, I think, between the kind of management challenges and leadership challenges that a leader faces and that leader's own impulses.
